chapters.title: React Rendering Performance, Lighthouse and Profiling
chapters.summary: Diagnose slow pages with Lighthouse, the Chrome Performance panel and the React Profiler, then fix wasted renders, long lists and blocking updates in React.

lesson.heading: A measurement-first workflow
lesson.body:
Performance work without measurement is guessing. A reliable loop:

- **Find the problem in field data**: which pages, devices and metrics are poor (CrUX, RUM with web-vitals attribution showing the LCP element or the slow interaction target)
- **Reproduce in the lab** with realistic conditions: DevTools CPU throttling (4x to 6x slowdown) and network throttling, a production build, a representative account and data size
- **Profile** to find the cause, fix one thing, re-measure, and confirm in the field after release

**Lighthouse** (in DevTools, PageSpeed Insights or Lighthouse CI) runs a simulated mobile page load and reports a performance score weighted mostly by TBT, LCP and CLS, plus FCP and Speed Index, along with diagnostics such as render-blocking resources, unused JavaScript and oversized images. Use the score as a trend indicator, not a goal in itself; the score varies between runs, so compare medians of several runs.

lesson.heading: Reading the Chrome Performance panel
lesson.body:
Record a trace while performing the slow interaction. Key parts:

- The **Main** track flame chart shows tasks on the main thread; tasks over 50 ms are marked as long tasks with red corners
- Each task breaks down into scripting (yellow), rendering and layout (purple) and painting (green); bottom-up and call tree tabs show which functions consumed the time
- The **Interactions** track shows each interaction with its input delay, processing time and presentation delay, mirroring INP
- Purple layout blocks with "Forced reflow" warnings point to **layout thrashing**: reading geometry (`offsetHeight`, `getBoundingClientRect`) after writing styles in the same loop
- The **Long Animation Frames (LoAF) API** reports long frames in the field with script attribution, so you can find the slow script in production

The DevTools Performance panel also shows live local Core Web Vitals and can compare them with CrUX field data for the URL.

lesson.heading: Why React components re-render
lesson.body:
A component re-renders when its **state changes**, when its **parent re-renders** (by default all children re-render, regardless of props), or when a **context** it reads changes. Rendering is calling your function and diffing the result; it only becomes a problem when it is expensive or very frequent (typing, scrolling, drag).

Use the **React DevTools Profiler** to record an interaction: it shows which components rendered, how long each took, and with "Highlight updates" and "Record why each component rendered" enabled, why.

Tools to avoid wasted work:

- `React.memo(Component)` skips re-rendering when props are shallowly equal
- `useMemo` caches an expensive computation or keeps an object reference stable; `useCallback` keeps a function reference stable for memoized children or effect dependencies
- **React Compiler** (stable since late 2025) memoizes components and values automatically at build time, making most manual useMemo/useCallback unnecessary in code it compiles

Often better than memoization: **move state down** to the component that uses it, or **lift content up** by passing children, so fewer components are affected by an update.

lesson.heading: Context, lists and keys
lesson.body:
**Context**: every consumer re-renders when the provider's value changes. A provider with `value={{ user, setUser }}` creates a new object each render, re-rendering all consumers. Memoize the value, split contexts by update frequency (for example state and dispatch separately), or use a store with selectors (Zustand, Redux, `useSyncExternalStore`) so components subscribe to slices.

**Long lists**: rendering thousands of rows costs DOM nodes, layout and memory. **Virtualize** with TanStack Virtual or react-window so only visible rows exist in the DOM. CSS `content-visibility: auto` lets the browser skip rendering off-screen sections with no JavaScript.

**Keys**: use stable, unique IDs. Index keys break state and cause extra work when items are inserted, removed or reordered, because React matches the wrong elements.

lesson.heading: Concurrent features and server rendering
lesson.body:
React 18+ can interrupt rendering so urgent updates (typing, clicking) are not blocked by expensive ones:

- `useTransition`: wrap a state update in `startTransition` to mark it non-urgent; React keeps the UI responsive and gives you `isPending` for feedback
- `useDeferredValue`: render with a lagging copy of a value, so an expensive list filters on the deferred query while the input updates instantly

These help INP directly by keeping input handling fast.

On the loading side: **Server Components** keep non-interactive UI off the client bundle, **streaming SSR with Suspense** sends HTML progressively so the shell and LCP content render before slow data arrives, and **selective hydration** prioritizes hydrating the parts users interact with. Avoid request waterfalls (component fetches data, renders child, child fetches) by fetching in parallel on the server or with route-level loaders.

keyPoints: Find problems in field data, reproduce with throttling on a production build, profile, fix, re-measure.
Lighthouse is a lab tool weighted mostly by TBT, LCP and CLS; treat its score as a trend, not the goal.
The Performance panel shows long tasks, interaction phases and forced reflows; LoAF attributes slow frames in the field.
React re-renders on state change, parent render or context change; the Profiler shows what rendered and why.
Prefer moving state down or passing children before memo, useMemo and useCallback; React Compiler automates memoization.
Split or memoize context values; virtualize long lists; use stable keys.
useTransition and useDeferredValue keep input responsive; Server Components and streaming improve loading.

questions.prompt: By default, what happens to child components when a parent re-renders in React?
options: Only children with changed props re-render
All children re-render unless they are memoized and their props are unchanged
questions.explanation: React re-renders the subtree by default. React.memo (or the React Compiler) is what enables skipping when props are equal.

questions.prompt: A memoized child still re-renders on every parent render. Its props are `onSelect={() => select(id)}`. Why?
options: A new function is created each render, so the shallow prop comparison fails
questions.explanation: Inline functions and object literals have new identities every render. Stabilize with useCallback or useMemo, or let the React Compiler handle it.

questions.prompt: Which code pattern causes forced synchronous layout (layout thrashing)?
options: Alternating reads of offsetHeight with style writes in a loop
questions.explanation: Each read after a write forces the browser to recompute layout immediately. Read everything first, then write, or use requestAnimationFrame.

questions.prompt: A table renders 10,000 rows and scrolling is janky. What is the most effective fix?
options: Virtualize the list so only visible rows are in the DOM
questions.explanation: The cost is mostly DOM size, layout and memory. Virtualization keeps a few dozen rows mounted regardless of data size.

questions.prompt: Typing in a search input feels laggy because each keystroke filters a large list. Which React API keeps the input responsive?
options: useDeferredValue (or startTransition for the filter update)
questions.explanation: Deferring the expensive render lets React handle the urgent input update first and interrupt the stale list render.

questions.prompt: Every consumer of an AuthContext re-renders whenever the provider's parent renders. What is the likely cause?
options: The provider value is a new object literal on every render
The context has a default value
questions.explanation: Context compares values by identity. Memoize the value with useMemo, or split state and actions into separate contexts.

questions.prompt: Wrapping every component in React.memo and every function in useCallback is a best practice that always improves performance.
questions.explanation: Memoization has its own cost and complexity and only helps when props are actually stable and renders are expensive. Profile first; the React Compiler can automate it safely.

questions.prompt: Lighthouse lab results can differ between runs, so you should compare several runs rather than a single score.
questions.explanation: Network and CPU variability, extensions and background work change results. Use medians and run on consistent hardware, as Lighthouse CI does.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which are reasons a React component re-renders?
options: A sibling's state changed (with no shared parent update)
The window was resized with no listener
questions.explanation: State, parent renders and consumed context trigger renders. Unrelated siblings and browser events without subscribed state do not.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: main-thread tasks longer than ___ ms are classified as long tasks.
questions.explanation: 50 ms comes from the RAIL model: to respond within 100 ms, a task should not occupy the thread for more than about 50 ms.

questions.prompt: How do you find and fix unnecessary re-renders in a React app?
questions.answer: I start with evidence: React DevTools Profiler with 'record why each component rendered', recording the slow interaction on a production-like build with CPU throttling. I look for components that render often and take significant time. Fixes in order of preference: restructure so fewer components depend on the changing state (move state down, pass expensive subtrees as children), fix context providers that create new value objects or split fast-changing context, subscribe to store slices with selectors, then React.memo for expensive children with stable props via useMemo and useCallback. If the project uses the React Compiler, much of the manual memoization is handled automatically. For big lists I virtualize. I verify with the Profiler and with INP in the field that the change helped.

questions.prompt: Walk me through debugging a slow interaction reported by users: clicking 'Apply filters' freezes the page for a second.
questions.answer:
- Confirm with field data (INP attribution from the web-vitals library or LoAF) which interaction and element, on which devices.
- Reproduce on a production build with 4x CPU throttling and record a Performance trace; the Interactions track shows input delay, processing and presentation.
- If processing is long, the flame chart shows which handlers and renders run: maybe filtering 20k items synchronously, a whole-page re-render through context, or a synchronous analytics call.
- If presentation delay is long, the DOM may be huge or layout is forced repeatedly.
- Fixes: update visible state first and yield, mark the heavy render as a transition, memoize or move filtering to a worker or the server, virtualize the results, batch DOM reads and writes.
- Re-measure in the lab, then watch INP after release.

questions.prompt: What do useTransition and useDeferredValue do, and when would you use each?
questions.answer: Both use concurrent rendering to mark some work as non-urgent, so React can keep urgent updates like typing responsive and interrupt stale renders. useTransition gives you startTransition to wrap a state update you control, plus an isPending flag, for example switching tabs or applying filters where the old UI can stay visible with a pending indicator. useDeferredValue takes a value and returns a version that lags behind during heavy renders; it is useful when you receive the value from props or cannot wrap the setter, such as rendering search results from a query. Neither makes the expensive work cheaper; they schedule it. If a single render is still very slow, I combine them with memoization, virtualization or moving work off the main thread.

chapters.title: Contrast, Screen Readers, Accessibility Testing and SEO Basics
chapters.summary: Meet color contrast requirements, test with real screen readers and automated tools, build accessibility into the development process, and cover the technical SEO fundamentals that overlap with it.

lesson.heading: Color and contrast
lesson.body:
WCAG contrast is a ratio between the relative luminance of foreground and background, from 1:1 to 21:1.

- **1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum), AA**: 4.5:1 for normal text; 3:1 for large text (at least 18 pt, about 24 px, or 14 pt bold, about 18.67 px)
- **1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced), AAA**: 7:1 normal, 4.5:1 large
- **1.4.11 Non-text Contrast, AA**: 3:1 for UI component boundaries and states (input borders, toggle states, focus indicators) and meaningful graphics (chart lines, icons)
- **1.4.1 Use of Color**: color cannot be the only way to convey information. A red border on an invalid field needs a text message or icon; links in body text need an underline or other non-color cue

Disabled controls and pure decoration are exempt. Check contrast for every state: hover, focus, placeholder text, text over images or gradients, and dark mode. Design tokens with pre-validated color pairs keep a whole product compliant. Remember Windows high contrast (forced colors) mode: use `forced-colors` media queries and avoid conveying state with background images only.

lesson.heading: How screen readers work and how to test with them
lesson.body:
Screen readers read the accessibility tree, not the pixels. Users navigate by headings (H key in NVDA and JAWS browse mode), landmarks, links, form fields and tables, or read linearly. They hear role, name, state and value: "Subscribe, checkbox, not checked".

The main combinations:

- **NVDA** (free) or **JAWS** with Chrome or Firefox on Windows
- **VoiceOver** with Safari on macOS and iOS (built in)
- **TalkBack** with Chrome on Android

A basic test script: navigate by headings and landmarks to understand the page structure; Tab through and check every control announces a sensible name, role and state; operate forms, including errors; open dialogs and menus; trigger dynamic updates and confirm they are announced. Listen for "unlabeled button", "clickable" divs, duplicated or missing announcements, and images announced by file name.

Visually hidden text (an `sr-only` class) provides extra context for screen readers without visual clutter, for example "Edit **invoice 1042**" instead of a row of identical "Edit" buttons.

lesson.heading: Automated accessibility testing and its limits
lesson.body:
Automated tools catch a meaningful share of issues quickly but cannot judge everything: whether alt text is accurate, focus order makes sense, or a custom widget is usable. Deque estimates axe-core finds around 57% of issues by volume; many experts quote 30-40% of WCAG criteria as automatable.

Layers to add:

- **Linting**: eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y catches missing alt, invalid ARIA, click handlers on non-interactive elements
- **Component tests**: Testing Library role queries plus `vitest-axe` or `jest-axe` assertions
- **E2E**: `@axe-core/playwright` scans full pages in real browsers, including states like open modals
- **Audits**: Lighthouse accessibility, axe DevTools, WAVE, and the browser accessibility tree inspector
- **Manual**: keyboard-only pass, screen reader pass, 200% and 400% zoom, reduced motion, and testing with disabled users when possible

Treat axe violations like failing tests in CI; a zero-violations baseline makes regressions visible immediately.

lesson.heading: Technical SEO fundamentals
lesson.body:
Search engines need to crawl, render, understand and rank your pages. Much of this overlaps with accessibility and performance.

- **Indexable HTML**: content and links should be in server-rendered or static HTML. Google renders JavaScript, but rendering may be delayed and other crawlers and social previews often do not run JS. Use real `<a href>` links so crawlers can follow them.
- **Titles and descriptions**: unique `<title>` per page with the main topic first; a meta description that summarizes the page (it affects click-through, not ranking directly)
- **Headings and semantics**: one clear `<h1>`, logical heading hierarchy, descriptive link text (not "click here"), alt text
- **Canonical URLs**: `<link rel="canonical">` to consolidate duplicates (tracking parameters, sorting variants)
- **Crawl control**: `robots.txt` controls crawling; `<meta name="robots" content="noindex">` controls indexing. Blocking a page in robots.txt does not remove it from the index and prevents Google from seeing the noindex.
- **Sitemaps** list canonical URLs; `hreflang` links language and region variants
- **Structured data** (JSON-LD with schema.org types like Product, Article, BreadcrumbList) can enable rich results
- **Page experience**: Core Web Vitals, HTTPS and mobile-friendliness are part of Google's ranking systems, though relevance matters far more

code.source:
<head>
  <title>Trail Running Shoes for Women | Acme Outdoor</title>
  <meta name="description" content="Lightweight, grippy trail shoes tested on rocky terrain. Free returns.">
  <link rel="canonical" href="https://acme.example/women/trail-shoes">
  <meta property="og:title" content="Trail Running Shoes for Women">
  <meta property="og:image" content="https://acme.example/og/trail.jpg">
  <script type="application/ld+json">
  {"@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": "Product", "name": "Ridge Runner 3",
   "offers": {"@type": "Offer", "price": "129.00", "priceCurrency": "USD"}}
  </script>
</head>

lesson.heading: Building accessibility and performance into the process
lesson.body:
Audits at the end of a project find hundreds of issues that are expensive to fix. Sustainable teams shift left:

- **Design**: accessible color tokens, focus styles, target sizes and annotated designs (heading levels, labels, focus order, error states) before development starts
- **Component library**: accessible primitives (dialogs, menus, comboboxes) built once on APG patterns or a proven headless library, documented in Storybook with the a11y addon
- **Definition of done**: keyboard operable, screen reader names checked, axe clean, performance budget met
- **CI**: lint rules, axe in component and E2E tests, Lighthouse CI and bundle budgets
- **Monitoring**: field Core Web Vitals and periodic manual audits against WCAG 2.2 AA, with an accessibility statement and a way for users to report problems

Overlay widgets that claim to make a site accessible with one script tag do not fix underlying issues and are widely criticized by disabled users and accessibility professionals.

keyPoints: AA contrast: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text and for UI components, focus indicators and meaningful graphics.
Never use color alone to convey information; add text, icons or underlines.
Test with real screen readers: NVDA or JAWS on Windows, VoiceOver on Apple, TalkBack on Android.
Automated tools (axe, Lighthouse, jsx-a11y) catch only part of the issues; manual keyboard and screen reader testing is required.
SEO basics: server-rendered content, real links, unique titles, canonical URLs, sitemaps, structured data and good Core Web Vitals.
robots.txt controls crawling, meta robots noindex controls indexing; do not combine them for the same page.
Shift left: accessible design tokens and components, definition of done, CI checks and field monitoring; avoid overlay widgets.

questions.prompt: What is the WCAG AA minimum contrast ratio for normal-size body text?
questions.explanation: 1.4.3 requires 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text at AA. 7:1 is the AAA enhanced level.

questions.prompt: Which WCAG criterion requires 3:1 contrast for input borders and focus indicators?
questions.explanation: Non-text Contrast covers visual information needed to identify components and their states, plus meaningful graphics.

questions.prompt: An invalid form field is shown only with a red border. Which criterion does this fail?
questions.explanation: Users who cannot distinguish red, and screen reader users, get no information. Add an error message in text, linked to the field.

questions.prompt: You want a page out of Google's index. What should you do?
options: Add <meta name="robots" content="noindex"> and allow crawling so Google can see it
Remove it from the sitemap only
questions.explanation: If robots.txt blocks crawling, Google cannot see the noindex directive and may keep the URL indexed from external links.

questions.prompt: Which screen reader and browser pairing is most representative on iOS?
questions.explanation: VoiceOver is built into iOS and is used with Safari (all iOS browsers use WebKit). TalkBack is Android's screen reader.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of `<link rel="canonical">`?
options: Telling search engines which URL is the preferred version among duplicates
questions.explanation: Canonicals consolidate ranking signals from parameter variants and duplicate URLs onto one preferred URL.

questions.prompt: If axe reports zero violations, the page is WCAG 2.2 AA compliant.
questions.explanation: Automated tools cannot evaluate many criteria, such as meaningful alt text, logical focus order or understandable error messages. Manual testing is required.

questions.prompt: Accessibility overlay widgets that inject a toolbar script are a reliable way to make a site compliant.
questions.explanation: Overlays cannot fix inaccessible markup and behavior at the source, can interfere with users' own assistive technology, and have not protected sites from lawsuits.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which practices help both accessibility and SEO?
options: Descriptive link text instead of 'click here'
A logical heading structure with one h1
Meaningful alt text on informative images
Hiding text in tiny gray font for keywords
questions.explanation: Clear structure and descriptive text help screen reader users and search engines understand content. Hidden keyword text is spam and harms both.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: structured data for rich results is usually added as a script of type application/___ using schema.org vocabulary.
questions.explanation: JSON-LD is Google's recommended structured data format because it is separate from visible markup and easy to generate.

questions.prompt: How do you test a web application for accessibility?
questions.answer:
- Automated checks in layers: eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y in the editor, axe assertions in component tests, @axe-core/playwright scans of key pages and states in E2E, and Lighthouse or axe DevTools for audits. These catch maybe a third to a half of issues.
- Keyboard-only pass through every flow: reachability, logical order, visible focus, no traps, dialogs and menus managing focus.
- Screen reader pass with at least NVDA plus Chrome and VoiceOver plus Safari: headings, landmarks, names, roles, states, form errors and live announcements.
- Visual checks: contrast in all states and themes, 200% and 400% zoom and reflow at 320 px, reduced motion, forced colors mode.
- Content review: alt text quality, link text, error messages.
- Ideally, usability sessions with disabled users, and an accessibility statement with a feedback channel.

questions.prompt: How would you make a client-rendered React SPA SEO-friendly?
questions.answer: The most robust step is rendering content on the server: move to a framework with SSR or static generation (Next.js, Remix/React Router, Astro) so each URL returns meaningful HTML, titles and meta tags without waiting for JavaScript. Each route needs a unique title, meta description, canonical URL and Open Graph tags, managed through the framework's metadata API. Navigation must use real anchor elements with href, not click handlers, so crawlers can discover pages. I would add an XML sitemap, a correct robots.txt, structured data where relevant, proper 404 status codes instead of soft 404s, and hreflang for localized versions. Then I would verify with Search Console's URL inspection to see the rendered HTML Google gets, and keep Core Web Vitals in good shape.

questions.prompt: Your company must reach WCAG 2.2 AA within six months on a large existing product. How do you plan it?
questions.answer: I would start with an audit of representative templates and critical flows (signup, checkout, account) using automated scans plus expert manual testing, producing issues mapped to WCAG criteria with severity. Since most issues come from shared components, I would fix the design system first: color tokens, focus styles, form fields, dialogs, menus and tables, which fixes many pages at once. Then fix critical flows by priority of user impact and legal risk. In parallel I would prevent new issues: lint rules and axe checks in CI, accessibility in the definition of done, design review checklists and training for designers, engineers and QA. Progress is tracked with an issue dashboard, and the plan ends with a re-audit, an accessibility statement and an ongoing process, since compliance is not a one-time project.
